alternative: Construct the shared object once in main and pass it to the values that need it (NewServer(cfg *Config), or a small interface) - plain Go dependency injection without package-scoped state; keep package-level var for immutable data only, and if the state really must be process-wide, wrap it in a sync.Mutex/atomic type whose methods own the synchronization.
idiom_name: package-scope var plus methods on a stateless struct (against Go's design guidance)
implementation_notes: Go has no static members, so the only way every value of a type can share state is to move the state out of the type entirely: package-level variables (initialized before main in dependency order) that ordinary struct methods read and write, with the structs themselves empty. What replaces the classic structure is package scope, and that is precisely what Go's own guidance rejects - package-scoped variables are process-wide singletons that smuggle state between unrelated concerns and make the code that relies on them hard to test, and go test -race plus order-dependent suites make the cost concrete. The classic form is defensible only for genuinely process-wide, mostly-read facilities such as a default logger configured once.
pitfalls: Package-level state is initialized by init() and dependency order before main and lives for the whole process: every test in the package shares it, so suites become order-dependent and go test -shuffle or -count=1 exposes the coupling.
Unprotected package state is a data race: go test -race flags concurrent access to a package-scoped map or field, and nothing in the type system prevents it.
init() side effects and registry-style package variables are this pattern at its most invisible; a library that mutates package state changes every program that imports it.
